claim: Resistance mutations against one drug can elicit collateral sensitivity against other drugs.
source: Resistance mutations against one drug can elicit collateral sensitivity against other drugs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon that motivates the study.

claim: Multi-drug treatments exploiting collateral sensitivity trade-offs can help slow down the evolution of resistance.
source: Multi-drug treatments exploiting such trade-offs can help slow down the evolution of resistance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known principle in the field.

claim: Many resistance mutations in Escherichia coli against various antibiotics have diverse collateral effects.
source: We show that many resistance mutations in Escherichia coli against various antibiotics indeed have diverse collateral effects.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1.

claim: Different experiments often produce collateral sensitivity profiles that are inconsistent with each other.
source: However, one important feature of these experimental studies has received little attention, namely, the fact that different experiments often produce collateral sensitivity profiles that are inconsistent with each other (e.g. Imamovic and Sommer, 2013; Oz et al., 2014; Barbosa et al., 2017; Maltas and Wood, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies showing inconsistent results.

claim: Wide variation in collateral outcomes is observed even between replicate populations.
source: However, wide variation in collateral outcomes is observed even between replicate populations (Oz et al., 2014; Barbosa et al., 2017; Maltas and Wood, 2019; Nichol et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental studies.

claim: For four out of six antibiotics used by Chevereau et al., 2015, between 12 (0.31%) and 170 (4.38%) knock-out mutations provide some level of resistance.
source: For four out of six antibiotics used by Chevereau et al., 2015, we find between 12 (0.31 %) and 170 (4.38%) knock-out mutations that provide some level of resistance against at least one of the antibiotics (false discovery rate (FDR) ∼25%; Figure 1, Figure 1—source data 1; see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the authors' analysis of published data, shown in Figure 1.

claim: E. coli likely have access to resistance mutations with diverse pleiotropic effects.
source: Since both data sets represent subsets of all resistance mutations, we conclude that E. coli likely have access to resistance mutations with diverse pleiotropic effects, such that a fitness gain in the presence of any one drug can come either with a pleiotropic gain or a pleiotropic loss of fitness in the presence of other drugs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the analysis of two datasets (knock-out and point mutation data).

claim: The JDFE framework is suitable for modeling the evolution of collateral resistance/sensitivity.
source: Therefore, the JDFE framework is suitable for modeling the evolution of collateral resistance/sensitivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed diversity of collateral effects.

claim: Positively correlated JDFEs sometimes lead to pleiotropic fitness losses.
source: Positively correlated JDFEs sometimes lead to pleiotropic fitness losses (Figure 2D,I), and negatively correlated JDFEs sometimes lead to pleiotropic fitness gains (Figure 2B,G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 2.

claim: Negatively correlated JDFEs sometimes lead to pleiotropic fitness gains.
source: Positively correlated JDFEs sometimes lead to pleiotropic fitness losses (Figure 2D,I), and negatively correlated JDFEs sometimes lead to pleiotropic fitness gains (Figure 2B,G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulations shown in Figure 2.

claim: JDFEs with apparently similar shapes can produce qualitatively different trajectories of pleiotropic fitness changes.
source: Overall, our simulations show that JDFEs with apparently similar shapes can produce qualitatively different trajectories of pleiotropic fitness changes (e.g. compare Figure 2A, F and B, G or Figure 2D,I and E,J).
evidence: This is a conclusion from simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: JDFEs with apparently different shapes can result in rather similar pleiotropic outcomes.
source: Conversely, JDFEs with apparently different shapes can result in rather similar pleiotropic outcomes (e.g. compare Figure 2B, G and E, J or Figure 2A,F and D,I).
evidence: This is a conclusion from simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The theory's predictions are valid in simulations in the SSWM regime.
source: We tested the validity of Equation 1 and Equation 2 by simulating evolution in the SSWM regime on 125 Gaussian JDFEs with various parameters (Materials and methods) and found excellent agreement (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is validated through simulations shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: The 1-1 rank correlation between c-rank and collateral resistance risk holds for all 125 Gaussian JDFEs and all population genetic parameters considered.
source: This 1–1 rank correlation holds more broadly, for all 125 Gaussian JDFEs and all population genetic parameters considered in the previous section (Figure 4C) as well as for the empirical TEM β-lactamase JDFEs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown through extensive simulations in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The correlation between estimated c-rank and actual collateral resistance risk is improved upon increased sampling.
source: As expected, this correlation is further improved upon increased sampling, and it is insensitive to the specific home fitness threshold that we use in the LD method (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown through simulations in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Estimating JDFE parameters is in principle feasible with a modest experimental effort, at least for the purpose of ranking drug pairs.
source: We conclude that estimating JDFE parameters is in principle feasible with a modest experimental effort, at least for the purpose of ranking drug pairs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the simulation results showing good ranking with small sample sizes.

claim: Treatments where drugs are chosen so that resistance against one causes sensitivity to the other can eliminate the population before multi-drug resistance emerges.
source: Treatments where the drugs are chosen so that resistance against one of them causes the pathogen or cancer population to become sensitive to the other—a phenomenon known as collateral sensitivity—can eliminate the population before multi-drug resistance emerges (Pál et al., 2015; Pluchino et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a known principle with supporting citations.

claim: The diversity of collateral effects among resistance mutations has rarely if ever been systematically measured.
source: However, the diversity of collateral effects among resistance mutations has rarely if ever been systematically measured.
evidence: This is an observation about the state of the field.

claim: Few existing approaches for designing robust multi-drug treatments have modelled mutational diversity explicitly within the population genetics context.
source: Moreover, few existing approaches for designing robust multi-drug treatments have modelled this mutational diversity explicitly within the population genetics context (Nichol et al., 2019; Maltas and Wood, 2019).
evidence: This is an observation about the state of the field with supporting citations.

claim: The JDFE is a local property of the fitness landscape which means it can be estimated by using modern high-throughput techniques.
source: Like the DFE, the JDFE is a local property of the fitness landscape which means that it can be, at least in principle, estimated by using a variety of modern high-throughput techniques (e.g. Qian et al., 2012; van Opijnen et al., 2009; Chevereau et al., 2015; Levy et al., 2015; Blundell et al., 2019; Aggeli et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a property of JDFEs with supporting citations to relevant techniques.

claim: The JDFE can change over time as the population traverses the fitness landscape.
source: The downside of this approach is that the JDFE can change over time as the population traverses the fitness landscape (Good et al., 2017; Venkataram et al., 2020; Aggeli et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation with supporting citations.

claim: In the context of collateral drug resistance and sensitivity, we are primarily interested in short time scales over which the JDFE can be reasonably expected to stay approximately constant.
source: However, in the context of collateral drug resistance and sensitivity, we are primarily interested in short time scales over which the JDFE can be reasonably expected to stay approximately constant.
evidence: This is a justification for the model's assumptions.

claim: No data sets are currently publicly available that would allow systematic exploration of the diversity of collateral effects among all resistance mutations against any one drug in any organism.
source: To our knowledge, no data sets are currently publicly available that would allow us to systematically explore the diversity of collateral effects among all resistance mutations against any one drug in any organism.
evidence: This is an observation about available data.

claim: Chevereau et al., 2015 measured fitness effects of 3883 gene knock-out mutations in E. coli in the presence of six antibiotics.
source: Instead, we examined the fitness effects of 3883 gene knock-out mutations in the bacterium Escherichia coli, measured in the presence of six antibiotics (Chevereau et al., 2015), as well as the fitness effects of 4997 point mutations in the TEM-1 β-lactamase gene measured in the presence of two antibiotics (Stiffler et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the data sources used in the study.

claim: Stiffler et al., 2015 measured fitness effects of 4997 point mutations in the TEM-1 β-lactamase gene in the presence of two antibiotics.
source: Instead, we examined the fitness effects of 3883 gene knock-out mutations in the bacterium Escherichia coli, measured in the presence of six antibiotics (Chevereau et al., 2015), as well as the fitness effects of 4997 point mutations in the TEM-1 β-lactamase gene measured in the presence of two antibiotics (Stiffler et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes the data sources used in the study.

claim: The JDFE is a natural extension of the DFE (distribution of fitness effects of new mutations).
source: The JDFE is a natural extension of the DFE, the distribution of fitness effects of new mutations, often used in modeling evolution in a single environment (King, 1972; Ohta, 1987; Orr, 2003; Kassen and Bataillon, 2006; Eyre-Walker and Keightley, 2007; Martin and Lenormand, 2008; MacLean and Buckling, 2009; Kryazhimskiy et al., 2009; Levy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a conceptual relationship with supporting citations.

claim: In the SSWM limit, a mutation that arises in the population either instantaneously fixes or instantaneously dies out.
source: In the SSWM limit, a mutation that arises in the population either instantaneously fixes or instantaneously dies out.
evidence: This is a defining property of the SSWM model.

claim: The dynamics of p(x,y,t) are well approximated by a diffusion equation when most mutations that contribute to adaptation have small effects.
source: However, if most mutations that contribute to adaptation have small effects, these dynamics are well approximated by a diffusion equation which can be solved exactly (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a theoretical approximation used in the model.

claim: Many microbes likely evolve in the 'concurrent mutation' regime, when multiple beneficial mutations segregate in the population simultaneously.
source: However, many microbes likely evolve in the 'concurrent mutation' regime, that is, when multiple beneficial mutations segregate in the population simultaneously (Desai and Fisher, 2007; Lang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a known phenomenon with supporting citations.

claim: A key characteristic of adaptation in the concurrent mutation regime is that mutations whose fitness benefits are below a certain 'effective neutrality' threshold fix with lower probabilities than predicted by Kimura's formula.
source: A key characteristic of adaptation in this regime is that mutations whose fitness benefits in the home environment are below a certain 'effective neutrality' threshold are usually outcompeted by superior mutations and therefore fix with lower probabilities than predicted by Kimura's formula (Schiffels et al., 2011; Good et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a known property of the concurrent mutation regime with supporting citations.

claim: A rigorous analytical calculation for ensemble variance in fitness even in the home environment is not yet available.
source: To our knowledge, a rigorous analytical calculation for ensemble variance in fitness even in the home environment is not yet available.
evidence: This is an observation about the state of theoretical knowledge.

claim: A direct way to validate the theory empirically would be to estimate JDFEs for a model organism in a number of drug pairs, rank these pairs according to the collateral rank statistic, and then test this ranking by evolving replicate populations.
source: A direct way to validate the theory empirically would be to estimate JDFEs for a model organism, such as E. coli, in a number of drug pairs, rank these pairs according to our collateral rank statistic and then test this ranking by evolving replicate populations and measuring the empirical distributions of collateral resistance/sensitivity outcomes.
evidence: This is a proposed experimental validation strategy.

claim: Antibiotic resistance JDFEs among genome-wide mutations have not yet been measured.
source: To the best of our knowledge, the antibiotic resistance JDFEs among genome-wide mutations have not yet been measured.
evidence: This is an observation about the state of empirical knowledge.

claim: Most evolution experiments have maintained too few replicate populations to accurately measure the variation in collateral outcomes of evolution.
source: Another obstacle is that, even though many researchers have experimentally evolved various microbes in the presence of drugs, most experiments have maintained too few replicate populations to accurately measure the variation in collateral outcomes of evolution.
evidence: This is an observation about the limitations of existing experimental work.

claim: The study by Nichol et al., 2019, with 60 replicates, is a notable exception to the typical low number of replicates.
source: The study by Nichol et al., 2019, with 60 replicates, is a notable exception.
evidence: This is a citation to an exceptional study.

claim: A rigorous test of the theory requires new data on the shapes of whole-genome JDFEs as well as higher throughput evolution experiments.
source: In short, a rigorous test of our theory requires new data on the shapes of whole-genome JDFEs as well as higher throughput evolution experiments.
evidence: This is a statement about what is needed to validate the theory.

claim: If empirical JDFEs resemble multivariate Gaussian distributions, then all relevant parameters can be learned by sampling a handful of random mutants.
source: For example, if empirical JDFEs resemble multivariate Gaussian distributions, then we can learn all relevant parameters of such JDFE by sampling a handful of random mutants and measuring their fitness in relevant environments.
evidence: This is a speculation about how JDFE estimation might work in practice.

claim: The model relies on the simplification that it describes the evolution of an asexual population where all resistance alleles arise from de novo mutations.
source: Our model relies on two important simplifications. It describes the evolution of an asexual population where all resistance alleles arise from de novo mutations.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the model.

claim: Some resistance alleles in bacteria may be transferred horizontally in reality.
source: In reality, some resistance alleles in bacteria may be transferred horizontally (Sun et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a known phenomenon with a supporting citation.

claim: Another major simplification is the assumption that the JDFE stays constant as the population adapts.
source: Another major simplification is in the assumption that the JDFE stays constant as the population adapts.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the model.

claim: In reality the JDFE will change over time because of the depletion of the pool of adaptive mutations and because of epistasis.
source: In reality the JDFE will change over time because of the depletion of the pool of adaptive mutations and because of epistasis (Good et al., 2017; Venkataram et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a known phenomenon with supporting citations.

claim: How JDFEs vary among genetic backgrounds is currently unknown.
source: How JDFEs vary among genetic backgrounds is currently unknown.
evidence: This is an observation about the state of knowledge.

claim: The main results hold at least in the presence of a simple form of 'global' epistasis.
source: In Appendix 1, we have shown that our main results hold at least in the presence of a simple form of 'global' epistasis.
evidence: This is stated as an extension of the theory shown in an appendix.

claim: The shape of JDFE must play a crucial role in determining whether the population evolves toward a generalist or diversifies into multiple specialist ecotypes.
source: While we were primarily motivated by the problem of evolution of collateral drug resistance and sensitivity, our theory is applicable more broadly. The shape of JDFE must play a crucial role in determining whether the population evolves toward a generalist or diversifies into multiple specialist ecotypes.
evidence: This is a broader implication of the theory.

claim: Previous literature has viewed the question of generalist vs. specialist evolution primarily through the lens of antagonistic pleiotropy and mutation accumulation hypotheses.
source: Previous literature has viewed this question primarily through the lense of two alternative hypotheses: antagonistic pleiotropy and mutation accumulation (Visher and Boots, 2020).
evidence: This is a summary of prior work with a citation.

claim: Antagonistic pleiotropy in its strictest sense means that the population is at the Pareto front with respect to home and non-home fitness.
source: Antagonistic pleiotropy in its strictest sense means that the population is at the Pareto front with respect to the home and non-home fitness, such that any mutation beneficial in the home environment reduces the fitness in the non-home environment (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a definition with a supporting citation.

claim: A population can evolve to become a home-environment specialist even in the absence of trade-offs, simply by accumulating mutations that are neutral in the home environment but deleterious in the non-home environment.
source: Alternatively, a population can evolve to become a home-environment specialist even in the absence of trade-offs, simply by accumulating mutations that are neutral in the home environment but deleterious in the non-home environment (Kawecki, 1994).
evidence: This is a known mechanism with a supporting citation.

claim: Antagonistic pleiotropy and mutation accumulation are not discrete alternatives but rather extremes of a continuum of models.
source: More recently, it has been recognized that antagonistic pleiotropy and mutation accumulation are not discrete alternatives but rather extremes of a continuum of models (Bono et al., 2020; Jerison et al., 2014; Jerison et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a recent perspective with supporting citations.

claim: The JDFE provides a mathematical way to describe the continuum between antagonistic pleiotropy and mutation accumulation.
source: The JDFE provides a mathematical way to describe this continuum.
evidence: This is a contribution of the current work.

claim: All JDFEs with negative r₂ lead to loss of fitness in the non-home environment and therefore can potentially promote specialization.
source: Our theory shows that in fact all JDFEs with negative r2 lead to loss of fitness in the non-home environment and therefore can potentially promote specialization.
evidence: This is a theoretical result from the model.

claim: The LD method is relatively easy to implement experimentally.
source: The LD method is relatively easy to implement experimentally, but it is expected to work only if the drug concentration is high enough to kill almost all non-resistant cells.
evidence: This is a practical observation about the LD method.

claim: The LD method is expected to work only if the drug concentration is high enough to kill almost all non-resistant cells.
source: The LD method is relatively easy to implement experimentally, but it is expected to work only if the drug concentration is high enough to kill almost all non-resistant cells.
evidence: This is a limitation of the LD method.

claim: Resistant mutants may be selected at concentrations much lower than MIC.
source: In reality, resistant mutants may be selected at concentrations much lower than MIC (Andersson and Hughes, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a known phenomenon with a supporting citation.

claim: Mutants selected at different drug concentrations may be genetically and functionally distinct.
source: Furthermore, mutants selected at different drug concentrations may be genetically and functionally distinct (Lindsey et al., 2013; Pinheiro et al., 2021) and therefore may have statistically different pleiotropic profiles.
evidence: This is stated as a known phenomenon with supporting citations.

claim: Mutants sampled with the LD method may not be most relevant for predicting collateral evolution at low drug concentrations.
source: As a result, mutants sampled with the LD method may not be most relevant for predicting collateral evolution at low drug concentrations, and other sampling methods may be required for isolating weakly beneficial mutations.
evidence: This is a limitation of the LD method inferred from the previous observations.

claim: Isolating individual weakly beneficial mutations is more difficult because by the time a mutant reaches a detectable frequency it has accumulated multiple additional driver and passenger mutations.
source: Isolating individual weakly beneficial mutations is more difficult because by the time a mutant reaches a detectable frequency in the population it has accumulated multiple additional driver and passenger mutations (Lang et al., 2013; Nguyen Ba et al., 2019), all of which can potentially have collateral effects.
evidence: This is stated as a known challenge with supporting citations.

claim: BLT allows one to sample mutants soon after they acquire their first driver mutation, before acquiring secondary mutations.
source: As a result, BLT allows one to sample mutants soon after they acquire their first driver mutation, before acquiring secondary mutations.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the BLT method.

claim: In a BLT experiment, each cell is initially tagged with a unique DNA barcode.
source: In a BLT experiment, each cell is initially tagged with a unique DNA barcode.
evidence: This describes how the BLT method works.

claim: As long as there is no recombination or other DNA exchange, any new mutation is permanently linked to one barcode in BLT.
source: As long as there is no recombination or other DNA exchange, any new mutation is permanently linked to one barcode.
evidence: This describes a property of the BLT method.

claim: A new adaptive mutation causes the frequency of the linked barcode to grow in BLT, which can be detected by sequencing.
source: A new adaptive mutation causes the frequency of the linked barcode to grow, which can be detected by sequencing.
evidence: This describes how adaptive mutations are detected in BLT.

claim: The correlation between estimated c-rank and actual ranking is insensitive to the specific home fitness threshold used in the LD method.
source: As expected, this correlation is further improved upon increased sampling, and it is insensitive to the specific home fitness threshold that we use in the LD method (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown through simulations in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.
